Thus $K^{(h)}$ is finite and symmetric, and for every $v$, $v^TK^{(h)}v=c_\sigma\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_i\sigma(G_i))^2]\ge0$. Because $G_i\sim N(0,1)$, its diagonal is $c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]=1$ by [F5]. This establishes the induction step.

For the fixed $H$, let $P(h)$ mean that $K^{(h)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for $0\le h<H$. Define $Q(k)$ to mean $P(j)$ for every $j\le\min(k,H-1)$. Step 1.1 gives $Q(0)$. If $Q(k)$ and $k+1<H$, step 2.1 applied with $h=k+1$ gives $P(k+1)$ and hence $Q(k+1)$; if $k+1\ge H$, $Q(k+1)$ adds no new index. By [F6], $Q(H-1)$ holds, so $K^{(H-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$; when $H=1$, this is exactly the base matrix $K^{(0)}$. By [F4], take independent $G,G'$ both distributed as $N_n(0,K^{(H-1)})$. The vector with coordinates $Y_i=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,G'_i\sigma'(G_i)$ has finite second moments; $\sigma'$ is bounded because it is the derivative of a Lipschitz differentiable function. Factoring expectations of independent variables gives $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)]=K_{ij}^{(H)}$. Therefore $K^{(H)}$ is finite and symmetric, and $v^TK^{(H)}v=\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_iY_i)^2]\ge0$ for every $v$. This proves the fully connected terminal claim and discharges that induction.

For the residual base layer let $G_0\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$ and $V^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,\sigma(G_0)$, with activation applied coordinatewise. Then $EV^{(1)}=b^{(1)}$ and $E[V^{(1)}(V^{(1)})^T]=S^{(1)}$ by [F1]. The growth bound used in step 2.1 proves finite second moments. Thus $S^{(1)}-b^{(1)}(b^{(1)})^T$ is its covariance, and its quadratic form in $v$ equals $E[(v^T(V^{(1)}-EV^{(1)}))^2]\ge0$.

The Gaussian expectation maps needed in the population recurrences are Lipschitz functions of the three entries of their bivariate covariance on any region $v\le Q_{ii},Q_{jj}\le Q$, where $v>0$ is fixed. Integrating this identity twice by parts gives the derivative of the expectation with respect to $\rho$ as $\sqrt{st}E[g'(U)g'(V)]$, where $g=\sigma$ or $g=\sigma'$. The boundary terms vanish because $g$ has at most linear growth and bounded first derivative; first integrate on finite rectangles and pass to the limit using the Gaussian tail and the displayed growth bounds. The same bounds extend to $\rho=\pm1$ by dominated convergence in the displayed representation. Finally $\rho=Q_{ij}/\sqrt{st}$ is Lipschitz in the entries when $s,t\ge v$. Write $\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}=\langle x_i^{(h)}(0),x_j^{(h)}(0)\rangle$ and, for residual layers, $\widehat b_i^{(h)}=m^{-1/2}\sum_r x_{i,r}^{(h)}(0)$.
